title: Fog over the road ahead
allegory: The discount factor is fog over the road ahead: a coin one step away looks γ times its size, two steps away γ² times, so distant coins fade from view, you effectively see about 1/(1 − γ) steps, and the fog is what keeps an endless road's total view finite.

cap.1: An agent walks a road that never ends, picking up a coin every step. Add it all up and every plan scores infinity. How do you tell a good plan from a bad one?
cap.2: In an endless task the plain sum of rewards can be infinite, so every policy ties. We also need a way to say that a reward now beats the same reward much later.
cap.3: Undiscounted returns diverge for continuing tasks with a nonzero reward rate, leaving values ill-defined; at γ = 1 the Bellman operator also loses its contraction property.

cap.1: Picture fog over the road. A coin one step ahead looks a bit smaller, two steps ahead smaller again. Far-off coins fade until they barely count.
cap.2: γ says how much a reward one step later is worth, between 0 and 1. A reward k steps ahead is worth γᵏ of its full value, and the return is the faded sum of everything ahead.
cap.3: Reward-to-go G_t = Σ_{i≥t} γ^(i−t) r_i. With |r| ≤ R_max and γ < 1 the sum is bounded by R_max/(1 − γ), so returns stay finite even for endless episodes.

chapters.name: The fading coins
chapters.title: What a coin k steps ahead is worth now, at γ = 0.9

cap.1: Each coin shrinks by the same fraction per step. With γ = 0.9, a coin ten steps away is worth about a third of one in hand.
cap.2: Present value is γᵏ times the reward. At γ = 0.9 that's 0.9, 0.81, 0.73 and so on, down to 0.35 at ten steps. The weights sum to 1/(1 − γ) = 10: roughly how far the agent sees.
cap.3: Σ_k γᵏ = 1/(1 − γ), the effective horizon: γ = 0.99 gives about 100 steps. In GAE, γ and λ compound: about 1/(1 − γλ) ≈ 17 steps at γ = 0.99, λ = 0.95.

cap.1: Thick fog (small γ) and the agent only cares about the next few coins. Thin fog (γ near 1) and it plans far ahead, but its sums get big and noisy.
cap.2: Small γ makes the agent short-sighted; γ near 1 makes it far-sighted, but its returns are larger and noisier to estimate. γ is a knob on how far ahead the agent optimises.
cap.3: Larger γ means longer credit assignment and higher-variance return estimates; smaller γ means myopic but easier targets. The optimal policy itself can change with γ.

chapters.name: The no-fog trap

right.title: no discount in RLHF
lines: every episode is the same length
γ would only rescale the reward

chapters.verdict: No fog is fatal on an endless road and harmless on a short, fixed one.

cap.1: Clear the fog completely on an endless road and the sums run away: planning never settles. On a short road of fixed length, though, you don't need fog at all.
cap.2: In the tabular exercises, γ = 1 stops the Bellman update contracting and makes (I − γP) singular, so evaluation never converges: keep γ < 1. RLHF episodes have a fixed length, so ARENA drops discounting there.
cap.3: For γ < 1 the Bellman expectation operator is a γ-contraction in sup norm: a unique fixed point and geometric convergence, and v = (I − γP)⁻¹r exists. With fixed-length episodes, γ only rescales a constant.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: γ sets how far ahead an agent plans
Keep γ < 1 in the tabular exercises

cap.1: When you train an agent, γ quietly decides how patient it is. Change it and you change which behaviour gets rewarded.
cap.2: γ turns up in returns, TD errors, value functions and GAE. Next week it compounds with λ in PPO's advantages; in RLHF it disappears because episodes are fixed length.
cap.3: Steering an agent through rewards means choosing its horizon too: the same reward function under a different γ can favour a different policy. Treat γ as part of the objective.

coda.title: One coin now, or a bigger coin later?

readouts.label: the agent would
readouts.f: B*pow(g, d) > 1 ? 'wait for the big coin' : 'grab the coin now'

caption.1: One coin now, or a bigger coin later? Slide the fog (γ) and the delay, and watch for the moment the agent stops being willing to wait.
caption.2: The orange curve is the big reward's present value, B·γᵈ, as the delay grows. Where it drops below the blue line the choice flips. Small γ makes the agent impatient; γ near 1 makes it wait.
caption.3: Prefer the delayed reward iff B·γᵈ > 1, that is d < ln B / ln(1/γ). The best policy depends on γ, so the horizon is part of the objective, not an afterthought.

hamming.what: A number γ between 0 and 1 saying how much a reward one step later is worth compared with the same reward now.
hamming.when: In every return, value function and TD update an RL agent computes, except fixed-length set-ups like ARENA's RLHF, which drop it.
hamming.why: It keeps infinite sums finite and evaluation convergent, and it sets how far ahead the agent effectively plans.

object.title: The fog staircase
object.subtitle: Five fogs side by side: each row is what a coin is worth now, at 0 to 11 steps ahead.

cap.1: Five fogs side by side. Each row shows what a coin is worth now at 0, 1, 2 and more steps ahead.
cap.2: Row r plots γᵏ for k = 0 to 11, for five values of γ.
cap.3: Each row is the discount kernel γᵏ; its sum over all k is 1/(1 − γ).

cap.1: Thick fog, γ = 0.5, wipes the road out within a few steps. Thin fog, γ = 0.99, barely fades over twelve.
cap.2: 0.5¹¹ is about 0.0005; 0.99¹¹ is about 0.9. Small differences in γ near 1 mean huge differences in horizon.
cap.3: Horizon scales as 1/(1 − γ): 2 steps at 0.5, 100 at 0.99, so γ is best thought of on a log scale near 1.

cap.1: For γ near 1, a coin about 1/(1 − γ) steps ahead has faded to roughly a third. That distance is how far the agent really sees.
cap.2: γ^(1/(1 − γ)) is close to e⁻¹ ≈ 0.37 when γ is near 1, which is why 1/(1 − γ) is called the effective horizon.
cap.3: ln γ ≈ −(1 − γ) near 1, so γ^(1/(1−γ)) → e⁻¹: the kernel's mean lookahead is about 1/(1 − γ).

cap.1: Turn on GAE's λ = 0.95 and every row fades faster, because the two fades multiply.
cap.2: GAE weights the TD errors by (γλ)ᵏ, so its lookahead is shorter than γ alone would give.
cap.3: A_t = Σ_l (γλ)^l δ_{t+l}: γ and λ compound multiplicatively into one kernel.

cap.1: At γ = 0.99 and λ = 0.95 the combined horizon is about 17 steps, not 100.
cap.2: 1/(1 − 0.99 × 0.95) ≈ 17: PPO's advantages look about 17 steps ahead with these standard settings.
cap.3: Effective horizon ≈ 1/(1 − γλ) ≈ 17 at γ = 0.99, λ = 0.95; λ = 1 recovers the full discounted return.

predict.q: Why does tabular policy evaluation fail to converge with γ = 1 on an endless task?

options.t: The Bellman update stops being a contraction, so there's no unique fixed point
The learning rate is too high

predict.why: γ < 1 shrinks the gap between estimates every sweep. At γ = 1 nothing guarantees that, and (I − γP) is singular.

predict.q: Why does ARENA's RLHF drop discounting?

options.t: Episodes are a fixed length from a fixed prompt, so γ would only rescale the reward

predict.why: With every episode the same length, discounting just multiplies one number by a constant.
